title: Cheaper per token, pricier per task (Bedrock cost per task and agent ROI)
caption:
Half the price per token. About 3x the cost per task. 🤔

AWS just published a worked example that every team running agents on Bedrock should see. Model A lists at $0.50 in / $1.50 out per 1M tokens. Model B lists at double that. On one agent task, A costs $0.0042 and B costs $0.00145 (illustrative prices, AWS's own example).

Why the "cheap" model loses:
- its tokenizer needs 50% more tokens for the same email
- it pads its JSON, so 450 output tokens instead of 150
- it misreads the tool schema and needs 3 turns, and every turn re-sends the whole history

The fix is to measure cost per successful task, not per call:
cost per attempt / success rate (retry until success), or cost per attempt + (1 - success rate) x escalation cost.

Then the harder question: is the agent better than the humans were? AWS's answer is boring and right. Measure the human baseline BEFORE launch, log every run with an experiment variant, human minutes and outcome, then compare against a holdout. Their scorecard starts at >90% tasks without rework for green and <75% for red, and they say to calibrate those yourself.

My take: the humanMinutes field is the sneaky one. Without it, "the agent did the work" quietly hides the 35 minutes a person spent reviewing it.

Save this for your next cost review 🔖 What is your agent's cost per successful task today? Tell me below.

Follow @shivanshu_builds for AI engineering on AWS, explained properly.

Source: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/optimizing-cost-per-task-and-proving-agent-roi-on-amazon-bedrock/

slides.headline: Half the price per token. ==~3x the cost== per task.
slides.sub: Why "cheaper model" is the wrong question, and how to prove an agent is worth it.

slides.title: Four ==hidden drivers== of your bill

cards.title: Tokenizer
cards.text: Same text, different token counts per model family.

cards.title: Verbosity
cards.text: Output often costs 3–5x input. Filler is pricey.

cards.title: Agent loops
cards.text: Every turn re-sends the whole history as input.

cards.title: Reasoning
cards.text: Thinking tokens bill as output, even if hidden.

slides.foot: None of these appear on the ==pricing page==.

slides.title: One task, ==two models==
slides.foot: AWS's ==illustrative== example. The 2x-priced model costs 65% less.

slides.title: Price the ==successful== task
slides.code:
# retry until it works
cost_per_success =
  cost_per_attempt / success_rate

# escalate on failure
cost_per_success = cost_per_attempt
  + (1 - success_rate) * escalation_cost
slides.foot: Cost per call flatters agents that ==loop==. Cost per success doesn't.

slides.title: Where the ==numbers== come from
slides.code:
# sketch: sum usage over one task's turns
for u in turn_usages:
    fresh += u["inputTokens"]
    read  += u["cacheReadInputTokens"]
    write += u["cacheWriteInputTokens"]
    out   += u["outputTokens"]
# price the 3 input buckets separately
slides.foot: With caching on, `inputTokens` is only the ==uncached== part. `CountTokens` compares tokenizers before you generate.

slides.title: Four ==levers== per task

items.title: Prompt caching
items.text: Cuts re-sent context. Biggest win on agent paths.

items.title: Prompt routing
items.text: Easy requests go to a cheaper model.

items.title: Batch inference
items.text: Halves the rate. No tools, no multi-turn.

slides.foot: Reasoning stays ==off== until a benchmark justifies it.
